name: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital: patient care and St. Jude Global (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: St. Jude Global's partner hospitals in more than 90 countries (94% of the result at the defaults, spread by world population: a judgment, the build names no split) and patient care in Memphis (6%).
summary: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital in Memphis treats about 1,000 new patients a year with childhood cancer and other catastrophic diseases, free to families, and through St. Jude Global supports children's cancer care at partner hospitals in more than 90 countries. For its fiscal year to June 2025 the two together come to about 0.01 years of healthy life per $1,000: St. Jude's own cost is about $1 million per new US patient, and its gain over the care these children would get at other US centres is a few points of survival, while St. Jude Global, 15% of the cost, brings most of the result. That is far below the site's global-health median (under a tenth of it) because these children would otherwise be treated at other US hospitals with nearly as good results, at US prices. The biggest uncertainties are how much St. Jude Global improves survival at partner hospitals (there is no controlled evaluation) and how much of St. Jude's survival advantage is case mix; the training and community programmes (about 6% of this model's spending, 3% of St. Jude's), which publish no outcomes, are valued at St. Jude's research result, discounted.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Programmes with no outcome data
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for a programme that publishes no outcome data at all: it is valued at the result per dollar of the same kind of work elsewhere on the site, read live, and counts less by the shared slider "How much we count a programme we could only estimate from similar ones" (docs/normalization.md 2.12). A programme with some outcome data is modelled from it in the chain above, with wide ranges, never here.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ programme expenses, both net of insurers' and grant money)
rows.explainer: Spreads fundraising and administration over the programmes St. Jude pays for itself: donations pay for all the fundraising, so the overhead goes on the own-funded spending only (1.74; 1.61 over all programme spending). Grants carry some indirect-cost recovery for the hospital's administration, so this slightly overstates the overhead on research.

rows.label: Patient care paid from St. Jude's own funds, FY2025
rows.explainer: Patient care less what insurers paid: $585.3 million, 81% of the cost of care.

rows.label: Share of the hospital's education and training that is St. Jude Global
rows.explainer: Judgment. The hospital's Form 990 says St. Jude Global's 'financial support will grow to $100 million annually by 2024' (Schedule H, Part VI, FY2024 return); its education and training line was $113.6 million that year and $146.2 million in FY2025, so Global (its Global Alliance, twinning with partner hospitals, training of partners' staff and the $200 million Global Platform for Access to Childhood Cancer Medicines run with WHO) is most of it: $105 million of $146 million at the best guess. The rest is the graduate school, fellowships, K-12 science programmes and community health work in Memphis, which publish no outcomes (the proxy section). Low if Global stayed at $80 million; high if nearly all growth went to Global and the Platform.

source.quote: Over the last three fiscal years (FY2019-FY2021) there were 2,637 new patients at St. Jude and its affiliate clinics.

rows.explainer: The latest published count of new patients, US patients only (international referrals are few). The hospital publishes no newer count; more than 9,300 patients are seen a year (combined accounts, note 1), most of them in follow-up or continuing outpatient care.

rows.label: Years the count covers

source.title: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, Community Health Needs Assessment 2022
source.quote: Over the last three fiscal years (FY2019-FY2021)

rows.explainer: FY2019 to FY2021.

rows.label: New patients a year in FY2025 against the FY2019-21 average
rows.explainer: Judgment. The pandemic held FY2020-21 down (national referrals fell from 21% to 15.6% of new patients with travel shut down, CHNA 2022 p. 10), and the FY22-27 strategic plan is expanding care: the hospital's Form 990 (FY2024, Schedule H) describes a $12.9 billion plan for 2,300 more jobs and two 15-storey towers for patient care and clinical research. The FY2025 accounts report more than 9,300 patients seen a year (note 1). 1.13 (13% more new patients than in FY2019-21); 1.0 if new patients didn't grow, 1.35 if the expansion added more new patients than follow-up visits.

rows.label: New patients a year, FY2025
rows.explainer: About 990 children a year start care at St. Jude. Each year's spending treats all children in care that year, new and continuing; in steady state that is one year's new patients carried through their whole treatment, so new patients a year are the flow one year's cost buys (Convention 3).

rows.label: Share of new patients with cancer

source.title: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, Community Health Needs Assessment 2022
source.quote: The majority of new St. Jude patients in FY2019-FY2021 have a primary diagnosis of childhood cancer (61.3%)

rows.explainer: The rest: blood disorders (20.1%), sickle cell disease (6.0%), HIV (3.2%) and other catastrophic diseases. Among the cancers, brain and nervous system tumours are 32%, leukaemia 25%, lymphoma 9.5%.

rows.label: Children with cancer treated a year at the partner hospitals St. Jude Global actively supports
rows.explainer: Judgment; St. Jude publishes no count of children reached. 'More than 500 member institutions and foundations around the world have joined the St. Jude Global Alliance', and St. Jude Global 'works directly with providers and institutions in more than 70 countries' (https://global.stjude.org/en-us/about/our-impact.html); a paediatric cancer unit in a middle-income country sees roughly 50 to 300 new patients a year (Ribeiro, Cancer Control 2014, describes a demonstration unit with about 200 new cases a year), and only some members get active programmes (twinning, nurse training, protocol adaptation, pathology support). The Global Platform for Access to Childhood Cancer Medicines, launched with St. Jude's $200 million in February 2025, began in six pilot countries and aims 'to reach 50 countries where needs are greatest' (UN News, https://news.un.org/feed/view/en/story/2025/02/1160036). Best: about 120 actively supported units at 200 children; low if active support reaches only a few dozen units, high if most members' patients benefit.

rows.label: People reached: new US patients and children at supported partner hospitals
rows.explainer: Both branches' people, for the canonical row and the cost per person.

rows.label: Cost per person reached (both branches)
rows.explainer: Context only: the two branches differ by two orders of magnitude (us_cost_per_patient, below).

rows.label: St. Jude's own cost per new US patient, overhead included
rows.explainer: About $1 million of St. Jude's own money (overhead included) per new patient over their treatment, on top of what insurers pay.

rows.label: Courses of treatment per new patient
rows.explainer: 1: each new patient gets one course of treatment, whose outcome is five-year survival; the rates below are over the course, not per year.

rows.label: Share of new cancer patients who would die within five years under standard US care

source.title: National Cancer Institute, Cancer in Children and Adolescents (fact sheet)
source.quote: 5-year survival was 83.2% for children younger than 1 year, 87.8% for children ages 1–4 years

rows.explainer: US five-year survival for childhood cancer is about 85-88% (2013-2019, by age; 87.3% at 15-19), so 12-15% die. St. Jude's mix has more brain tumours (32% of its new cancer patients) and more referred high-risk cases than the national mix, so 15% (12-20%). The baseline mortality the survival gain below is a share of; it is the rate over a course of treatment, not a yearly rate.

rows.label: Cut in five-year deaths at St. Jude against standard US care, cancer patients (relative)
rows.explainer: Judgment, anchored on the one like-for-like comparison: in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, St. Jude's Total XV trial (2000-07, 498 patients) reached 93.5% ± 1.9% five-year survival against 90.4% ± 0.5% in the Children's Oncology Group's trials (2000-05, 7,153 patients; Pui et al., J Clin Oncol 2015, Table 1, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4567699/): deaths 6.5% against 9.6%, a third fewer. The other leading groups sit between (DFCI 91%, UKALL 91.6%). For the whole cancer mix a quarter fewer deaths: brain and solid tumours (two-thirds of St. Jude's cancer patients) have no comparable published comparison, and nine in ten US children with cancer are treated at Children's Oncology Group centres on the same or similar protocols, many developed at St. Jude. 0 if the gap is case mix; 40% if the solid-tumour and brain-tumour programmes (proton therapy, its own neuro-oncology trials) do as well as leukaemia's best. How far the comparison is confounded is in internal_validity_adj, not here.

rows.label: Share of other new patients (blood disorders, sickle cell, HIV) who would die within five years under standard US care
rows.explainer: Judgment. Most of these children have non-malignant blood disorders, sickle cell disease or HIV, with five-year mortality of a few per cent in US care; a minority have bone-marrow failure or immune disorders treated by transplant, with higher risk.

rows.label: Cut in five-year deaths at St. Jude against standard US care, other patients (relative)
rows.explainer: Judgment: less than the cancer cut, since sickle cell and HIV care follow national guidelines St. Jude shares with other centres; 0 to 30% (transplant outcomes).

rows.label: Deaths averted per new US patient (before adjustments)
rows.formula: us_cancer_share * us_cancer_mortality_alternative * us_cancer_mortality_reduction + (1 - us_cancer_share) * us_noncancer_mortality_alternative * us_noncancer_mortality_reduction
rows.explainer: Baseline deaths × the cut, weighted by the diagnosis mix: about 2.4 deaths averted per 100 new patients.

rows.label: Share of new US patients who would die within five years under standard care
rows.explainer: The diagnosis mix's baseline.

rows.label: Share of children at supported partner hospitals who would die without the partnership's improvements
rows.explainer: Judgment. Survival from childhood cancer is about 20-30% in low-income countries ('an overwhelming 70 per cent death rate', UN News on the Global Platform's launch, https://news.un.org/feed/view/en/story/2025/02/1160036) and more than 80% in high-income ones; St. Jude's partners are mostly referral hospitals in middle-income countries, where 40-60% survive.

rows.label: Cut in deaths at supported partner hospitals from the partnership (relative)
rows.explainer: Judgment. The published before-and-after results of St. Jude's twinnings: in Recife, Brazil, five-year event-free survival from acute lymphoblastic leukaemia rose from 32% (1980-89) to 63% (1997-2002) among 375 children, with abandonment of treatment within a year falling from 16% to 0.5% (Howard et al., JAMA 2004;291:2471-5, https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.291.20.2471); events there count relapse, toxic death and abandonment, so deaths fell by less than the 46% drop in events. St. Jude's goal for a new partner is 'to quickly achieve a 60% event-free survival rate', from rates that start below 10% to 60% depending on the country (Ribeiro, Cancer Control 2014, https://www.cancercontrol.info/wp-content/uploads/2014/08/106-110-Ribeiro.pdf). These are the intensive, long twinnings of the first 19 sites, for leukaemia, the most curable cancer; the average Alliance member now gets lighter support (training, protocols, consultations, medicines) for all its cancers. No results at other partner sites are published that would make a reference class across partners; Ribeiro notes that acute myeloid leukaemia and brain tumours 'remain challenging at many partner sites'. 12% fewer deaths on average (6 points at a 50% baseline), 2% for light support of units treating mostly hard cancers, 30% for twinnings like Recife. Before the counterfactual (the background trend) and the evidence discount.

rows.label: Deaths averted per child at supported hospitals (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Baseline deaths × the cut.

rows.label: Baseline mortality over a course of treatment, US patients (the main branch; for reading)
rows.explainer: Mortality over a course of treatment (not a yearly rate) in the main branch by spending, the US patients; the global branch's is gl_baseline_mortality.

rows.label: Cut in deaths, US patients (the main branch; for reading)
rows.explainer: Deaths averted as a share of baseline deaths in the US branch (the global branch's is gl_mortality_reduction).

rows.label: Deaths averted per new US patient (the main branch; for reading)
rows.explainer: The US branch's figure (the global branch's is gl_deaths_averted_per_child); each branch uses its own.

rows.label: Indirect deaths per direct death averted
rows.explainer: 0: the survival gains are all-cause survival, so no deaths come on top.

rows.label: US deaths averted: share under five
rows.explainer: Judgment from the age of new patients (CHNA 2022, Figure 6, p. 13): under 2, 22.6%; 2 to under 5, 16.8%; 5-9, 17.8%; 10-14, 20.9%; 15-19, 18.7%; 20 and over, 3.2%. 39% are under five at diagnosis, but a death averted comes one to five years later (benefit_midpoint_years), so the diagnoses at 3-4 (about two-fifths of the 2-to-under-5 group, 7% of patients) mostly die, if they do, after five: about 30% of deaths averted fall under five.

rows.label: US deaths averted: share aged 5 to 14 among those five and over
rows.explainer: Judgment from the same figure: of patients five and over at diagnosis, 63% are 5-14; deaths averted come a little later, and patients diagnosed at 3-4 move into this band, so 60%; the rest at 15-49.

rows.label: US deaths averted: share aged 15 to 49 among those 15 and over
rows.explainer: 1: St. Jude treats patients up to about 21 (only 3.2% of new patients are 20 or older), so no death averted falls at 50 or over.

rows.label: Partner hospitals' deaths averted: share under five
rows.explainer: Judgment: partner units are paediatric (mostly 0-14); leukaemia and the embryonal tumours peak at 2-5. Under five: 30% of deaths averted.

rows.label: Partner hospitals' deaths averted: share aged 5 to 14 among those five and over
rows.explainer: Judgment: paediatric units take children up to 14 or 18 depending on the country.

rows.label: Deaths averted: share under five, both branches (for reading only)
rows.explainer: Weighted by each branch's deaths averted; each branch values its deaths with its own ages.

rows.label: Deaths averted: share 5 to 14 of those five and over, both branches (for reading only)
rows.explainer: Weighted by each branch's deaths averted.

rows.label: Deaths averted: share 15 to 49 of those 15 and over (for reading only)
rows.explainer: 1 in both branches: no death averted falls at 50 or over.

rows.label: Illness averted, as a share of the value of deaths and income
rows.explainer: 0: illness is counted in DALYs instead (dalys_illness_averted_per_person and the bridge), never both. GiveWell's shares are for prevention in poor countries and don't apply here.

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per person reached
rows.explainer: 0: a children's hospital doesn't avert stillbirths.

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person, ln(consumption) a year
rows.explainer: 0: a survivor's later earnings are part of the value of the life saved (the moral weight); St. Jude's patients aren't a population with evidence of a developmental income effect like malaria or deworming.

rows.label: Years until the income gain starts
rows.explainer: No income gain is counted (ln_income_gain_per_year is 0), so no wait applies; none of the site's figures (malaria, SMC, iron, deworming) fits this programme.

rows.label: Years the long-term income gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how long a long-term income gain lasts (GiveWell's working years, 40), read by every model that counts one (INV-13).

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person reached, present value
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate, the wait included, so the result moves with it. Never type in a present value worked out elsewhere: rebuild it from its inputs.

rows.label: Resource sharing within households (multiplier on an earner's gain)
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (GiveWell's): an earner's income gain is shared with the household, so it counts this many times. Read by every model that values a long-term income gain (INV-13).

rows.label: Share of new US patients spared a lasting late effect they would have had at another centre
rows.explainer: Judgment. Survivors of childhood cancer carry late effects (heart, hearing, fertility, neurocognitive); St. Jude's proton therapy for brain tumours and its survivorship clinic aim to cut them, but the protocols that reduce late effects (no cranial irradiation in leukaemia, risk-adapted doses) are now standard at other centres too. 3% of patients spared one; 0 if other centres match St. Jude, 10% if proton therapy spares many brain-tumour survivors (a third of cancer patients).

rows.label: Disability weight of a typical late effect
rows.explainer: Judgment anchored on GBD 2019 disability weights for the commonest late effects: moderate hearing loss 0.027, mild heart failure 0.041, mild intellectual disability 0.043, moderate 0.1 (GBD 2019 disability weights, IHME).

rows.label: Years a late effect lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment: from the end of treatment in childhood through most of adult life; discounted in us_dalys_illness_per_patient.

rows.label: Illness averted per new US patient over standard care, in DALYs
rows.explainer: Patients spared × the disability weight × the years it would have lasted, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Illness averted per person reached, in DALYs (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The US branch's illness averted spread over all people reached, for reading; the bridge uses the branch's own figure. None is counted for the partner hospitals, where deaths are the outcome measured.

rows.label: What a family would pay out of pocket in a year of treatment elsewhere (medical bills, travel, lodging, food), 2018 dollars

source.title: Iragorri et al., The Out-of-Pocket Cost Burden of Cancer Care: A Systematic Literature Review, Current Oncology 2021

rows.explainer: St. Jude bills no family and pays travel, housing and meals for the patient and a parent. At another hospital a family pays deductibles and co-payments (none for the 41% on Medicaid) and its own travel and lodging. The review gives paediatric cancer patients USD 800 a month, pooled across high-income countries (2018 dollars; likely low for the US, where adult patients and caregivers spend $180 to $2,600 a month): $800 × 12 = $9,600 a family-year of active treatment, $3,000 (Medicaid families near the centre) to $20,000. Lost parental earnings aren't counted, since St. Jude doesn't replace them either.

rows.label: The same, in 2024 dollars
rows.explainer: In the prices of the year modelled (Convention 8), US consumer prices (World Bank).

rows.label: Years of active treatment the family costs cover
rows.explainer: Judgment: leukaemia treatment lasts 2-3 years (most of it outpatient), solid and brain tumours about a year, other patients' care is lighter; 1.5 years on average.

rows.label: Share of those costs no one else would have covered
rows.explainer: Judgment: at other centres some families get help with lodging (Ronald McDonald Houses), travel and bills from hospital financial counselling and childhood-cancer charities; 70% of the costs would have stayed with the family.

rows.label: Consumption gain per family member in a treatment year, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: The family's saving as a share of an average US household's consumption (2.4 people at $58,517 each, World Bank 2024): about 8%, on the site's one log scale. The saving is valued like cash (the cash-income family's chain).

rows.label: US branch: evidence adjustment on the survival gain
rows.explainer: The product of its two parts.

rows.label: External validity (US branch): the comparison's setting against St. Jude's today
rows.explainer: 1: the comparison is between US centres treating US children, the setting of this branch; how far the trials measured a real difference is in internal_validity_adj.

rows.label: Internal validity (US branch): how far the comparison measures St. Jude's own effect
rows.explainer: Judgment. The survival gain comes from comparing trials run by different groups, not from randomising children between centres: St. Jude's trial patients may differ from the Children's Oncology Group's in risk and in who enrols, and its results spread to other centres within years. 0.6, the GiveWell-style discount for a non-randomised comparison (its internal-validity adjustments for observational evidence run 0.5-0.7); 1 if the 3-point gap is all St. Jude's care.

rows.label: US branch: share of the gain that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the survival gain is already the difference from the care these children would otherwise get (other US centres), so nothing more is taken off for what would have happened anyway (Convention 5).

rows.label: US branch: St. Jude's share of the resources behind the care
rows.explainer: St. Jude's own funds ÷ the full cost of care; insurers paid the rest (Convention 2). Their payments buy care these children would get elsewhere anyway, which the survival gain already nets out, so a higher share is arguable; 81% follows the site's rule.

rows.label: US branch: share of patients counted who get the care as studied
rows.explainer: 1: the patients counted are the patients St. Jude treated.

rows.label: Would others have paid for this anyway (below 1), or does the money pull others in (above 1)?
rows.explainer: Judgment. No government or other funder would step in for St. Jude's own funds; its reserves (gift_to_grant_years) are counted as a wait, not as funging. 0.9 if the reserves mean a marginal donation mostly substitutes for investment returns St. Jude would spend anyway.

rows.label: Global branch: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Judgment. The only outcome evidence is before-and-after survival at a few partner hospitals, without control sites, and the gain per child is itself a judgment; 0.5, below the US branch's 0.6 because there is no comparison group at all.

rows.label: Global branch: share of the improvement that wouldn't have come anyway with no partnership at all
rows.explainer: Judgment: the background trend only. Survival from childhood cancer in middle-income countries rises over a partnership's decade without any partner too, with national cancer plans, health spending and economic growth; about 30% of the improvement at partner units would have come anyway. Other partners' and local funders' contributions are not taken off here: they are resources behind the improvement, in gl_attribution_share (Convention 5, one question per adjustment).

rows.label: Local spending per child treated at partner hospitals (governments, hospitals, local foundations, families)
rows.explainer: Judgment, anchored on the costing studies in the systematic review of childhood cancer treatment in low- and middle-income countries (Fung et al., BMJ Global Health 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6830048/): for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in middle-income countries about $5,700 a patient (Bangladesh), $9,300-16,900 (Iran), $21,000-24,800 (Mexico) and $6,400-44,700 (China); for all cancers about $10,500 (Ghana) and $30,000 (El Salvador) per newly diagnosed patient a year (2018 US$). $10,000 for the partner units' mix; $3,000 for lower-middle-income units, $25,000 for upper-middle-income units on full leukaemia protocols. A check: St. Jude's own direct financial contribution falls to about 3-4% of a mature partner unit's budget (Ribeiro, Cancer Control 2014, https://www.cancercontrol.info/wp-content/uploads/2014/08/106-110-Ribeiro.pdf), though it is the largest part at the start, and St. Jude's staff time comes on top.

rows.label: Other international partners' spending per child at the same hospitals (other twinning centres, NGOs, drug donations)
rows.explainer: Judgment: other high-income twinning partners (European and Canadian centres, SIOP programmes), international NGOs and drug donation programmes also support many St. Jude partner units, with smaller budgets than St. Jude Global's; about a tenth of local spending. Anchor: St. Jude's own direct financial contribution falls to 3-4% of a mature unit's budget (Ribeiro 2014), and other external donors are of the same order or smaller, so $1,000 (about 10% of the $10,000 local cost) allows for several of them; $300 to $3,000.

rows.label: Global branch: St. Jude's share of the resources behind the care at partner hospitals
rows.explainer: St. Jude Global's cost ÷ its cost plus what governments, hospitals, local foundations, families and other international partners spend treating these children (Convention 2).

rows.label: Global branch: share of children counted who get the improved care
rows.explainer: 1: the reach is already the children at actively supported units; how much of the improvement reaches them is in the survival gain.

rows.label: Cash and investments at 30 June 2025

source.title: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital and ALSAC, combined financial statements, years ended June 30, 2025 and 2024 (audited, Deloitte & Touche LLP)
source.page: p. 3, combined statements of financial position (in 000s)
source.quote: CASH AND CASH EQUIVALENTS $ 557,709 ... UNRESTRICTED INVESTMENTS 8,444,862 ... RESTRICTED INVESTMENTS 1,587,521

rows.explainer: Cash ($557.7 million), unrestricted investments ($8,444.9 million) and investments restricted by donors ($1,587.5 million): about three and three-quarter years of spending held in reserve.

rows.label: Years a donation waits before St. Jude spends it
rows.explainer: The reserves ÷ a year's spending, as the template asks for a charity that spends from reserves: 3.7 years. St. Jude holds its reserves by policy and spends from donations, bequests and investment returns, so a dollar given today adds to the pool and is, on average, spent about this much later. While it waits it is invested (interest_yield), which almost cancels the discount.

rows.label: Long-run nominal return on the invested reserves
rows.explainer: Judgment. The reserves earned $939.3 million in FY2025 on about $9.6 billion of investments (p. 4; average of the two year-ends, p. 3), 9.7%, and $856.7 million in FY2024: two strong market years. Long-run returns of diversified endowment portfolios have averaged about 6-7% a year nominal over ten-year periods (US college and university endowment studies, NACUBO-Commonfund); 6.5%, 4% in a weak decade, 9% at the recent returns.

rows.label: Yearly rise in the cost of care and research
rows.explainer: Judgment: US medical-care prices have risen about 3% a year over the past two decades (BLS consumer price index for medical care), a little faster than general inflation; what a dollar held in reserve buys later falls by this much a year.

rows.label: Real return on the invested reserves while a donation waits
rows.explainer: The return in what it buys: the benefit a later dollar buys is valued in today's care.

rows.label: Years from the spending to the care
rows.explainer: 0: the spending is the year's care and support itself.

rows.label: Years from treatment to the middle of the deaths averted
rows.explainer: Judgment: the children who would have died without the better care die mostly of relapse or treatment toxicity within five years of diagnosis, more of them early; two years to the middle.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the benefits come
rows.explainer: Every wait is discounted at the shared rate; the reserves earn their real return while a donation waits (interest_yield).

rows.label: US branch: all adjustments combined
rows.formula: us_evidence_adj * us_counterfactual_adj * us_attribution_share * us_implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount
rows.explainer: The product of the US branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Global branch: all adjustments combined
rows.formula: gl_evidence_adj * gl_counterfactual_adj * gl_attribution_share * gl_implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount
rows.explainer: The product of the global branch's adjustments.

rows.explainer: Each branch applies its own.

rows.label: All adjustments combined, outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.explainer: Each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Treatment costs averted, as a share of value
rows.explainer: 0: this is treatment, not prevention. Insurers and Medicaid would pay another hospital for the same child, but they also pay St. Jude ($141.3 million, at prospective rates like any hospital's), so what they save is at most the gap between the two hospitals' rates, which isn't published; it is a transfer between payers, not a health gain, and isn't counted.

rows.label: Rebound in illness from lost immunity
rows.explainer: 0: malaria prevention only.

rows.label: Income gains invested and paying off later
rows.explainer: 0: no later-life income gain is counted, and a family's saved costs during treatment are consumed, not invested.

rows.label: Other effects not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Judgment: psychosocial care, school and family support during treatment, and partner hospitals' better care for children with other diseases (positive); St. Jude Global's staff drawn from other duties at partner hospitals (negative). The knowledge St. Jude's patient care produces through its trials is counted in the research model, not here.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The supplementary shares, each its own row, summed.

rows.explainer: The US branch's illness averted, with its adjustments.

rows.explainer: The bridge from DALYs into units of value: the unit's conversion cancels it, so illness counts as healthy years whatever "Healthy year vs doubled-income year" is set to.

rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights for the age band of each death, times your multiplier on the value of a life: the site's one value of a death (docs/normalization.md 2.7), the same for a child in Memphis as anywhere.

rows.label: Value of a death averted at partner hospitals (units of value)
rows.explainer: The same weights for the partner hospitals' age mix; no death averted there falls at 50 or over.

rows.explainer: The deaths-weighted average of the two branches' values (GiveWell's moral weights by age band × $life_value_multiplier).

rows.label: Units of value from stillbirths averted

rows.explainer: 0 (no later-life income gain is counted), on the site's one log scale.

rows.label: Units of value from illness averted
rows.explainer: A share of the deaths' and income's value, the base GiveWell's supplementary share has.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until families' costs are covered
rows.explainer: The reserves' wait only: the savings come during treatment, whose years pv_annuity_due already discounts (not at the middle of the deaths averted).

rows.label: Units of value from families' costs covered (US branch)
rows.formula: us_new_patients * @household_size.united_states * us_ln_gain_per_person_year * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, us_treatment_years) * us_family_cost_counterfactual * cash_wait_discount * $uov_per_ln_consumption
rows.explainer: The care is free to families, as cash to them would be (templates.md, direct-health: cash handed out with the service is valued as the cash-income family does): every member of the household gains the saving on the log scale, for the years of treatment, discounted. St. Jude pays it from its own funds, so no co-funder's share comes off.

rows.label: Total units of value
rows.formula: (uov_deaths + uov_stillbirths + uov_income + uov_cash) * (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj) + uov_morbidity + uov_from_daly
rows.explainer: Deaths, families' costs covered and the supplementary shares, plus illness counted in DALYs through its bridge.

rows.label: Spending on programmes with no outcome data: the hospital's training, graduate school and community programmes, FY2025
rows.explainer: The rest of the hospital's education and training after St. Jude Global: the graduate school, postdoctoral and clinical fellowships, nursing externships, K-12 science clubs and the Memphis community health programmes (HPV vaccination awareness, HIV prevention outreach). St. Jude reports activities (students, schools) but no outcomes, so they are valued at a comparable programme (Convention 12). Not part of program_spend.

rows.label: Result per dollar of comparable programmes on the site (units of value per dollar you give)
rows.explainer: The nearest evaluated programme: St. Jude's own research (its model, read live). Most of this spending is the graduate school and postdoctoral and clinical fellowships, which train researchers and clinicians for the same field: research capacity. No training programme is evaluated on the site; the K-12 science clubs and Memphis awareness programmes (HPV vaccination, HIV prevention) are a small part with no closer evaluated peer either.
